title: A Reconfigurable Multilayer Quantum Key Distribution Network over Existing Metropolitan Fibre
authors: Mariella Minder, Andreas Siakolas, Elizabeth Pasatembou, Stylianos Mavrikos, Stephanos Yerolatsitis, Konstantinos Katzis, Kyriacos Kalli
abstract: Scaling quantum networks requires architectures extending end-to-end service reachability despite constrained fibre and equipment. Critically, in brownfield deployments, the quantum network must be engineered around classical telecommunications infrastructure and the operating capabilities of quantum key distribution (QKD) technology. To address this, we demonstrate a seven-node, multilayer QKD network deployed over existing metropolitan fibre. The implementation compares spectral management techniques to accommodate inherited constraints across its layers. It combines a trusted-node ring with a three-node subnetwork interconnected through reconfigurable optical switching, extending physical connectivity and service reachability without an additional transmitter. A meshed key management layer maps endpoint requests onto trusted-relay paths and supplies Layer 1, Layer 3, and one-time-pad applications. Over 73 days, eight link configurations generated 119.4 Gbit of secret key material with 99.1% link availability. Randomised end-to-end requests revealed indirect cross-layer coupling between key consumption, stored-key state and quantum-layer reconfiguration, demonstrating resource sharing through reconfigurability, spectral multiplexing and logical key-management abstraction.
summary: This paper details the deployment and testing of a complex, multi-layer Quantum Key Distribution network over existing metropolitan fibre. By combining a trusted-node ring with a reconfigurable subnetwork, the authors achieved high key generation rates and demonstrated resource sharing across layers. This work is significant for showing how quantum networks can be practically scaled in real-world, constrained environments.
main_problem: Scaling quantum networks requires architectures that maintain end-to-end service reachability despite constrained physical fibre and equipment, especially in brownfield deployments.
main_result: The implemented multi-layer QKD network successfully demonstrated resource sharing and high availability (99.1%) over 73 days by integrating a trusted-node ring and a reconfigurable subnetwork.
method: The study involved deploying and monitoring a seven-node, multi-layer QKD network over existing metropolitan fibre, using SDN control to manage key requests across multiple physical layers.
model_or_system: The system is a seven-node, multi-layer QKD network built over existing metropolitan fibre, comprising a quantum layer (trusted-node ring and reconfigurable subnetwork), a Key Management Layer (KMS), and an application layer for services like Layer 1 and Layer 3 encryption.
key_observables: Secret Key Rate (SKR), Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER), Link Availability (99.1%), and Reconfiguration Overhead (17 +/- 5 minutes).
important_parameters: 73-day monitoring period; 119.4 Gbit of secret key material generated; 133% increase in logical endpoint-pair reachability.
main_assumptions: The logical reachability is subject to sufficient stored key material on each physical link and the security assumptions of the trusted nodes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the multi-layer architecture (physical, logical KMS, application), and time-series plots show key rate and QBER stability over the 73-day deployment period.
paper_structure: The paper details the physical deployment, the multi-layer architectural design (Quantum, KMS, Application), the spectral management techniques used for integration, and finally, long-term performance measurements and overhead characterization.
why_interesting: The work provides a concrete, large-scale demonstration of integrating quantum communication into existing classical infrastructure, which is a major engineering hurdle for quantum networking.

Fig. 3h shows the temporal evolution of the QBER. The arithmetic mean of the eight per-link temporal mean QBER values was 1.2%, with a standard deviation across link configurations of 0.2%. QBER remained within a narrow operating range during key-generation periods, with individual-link temporal means between 0.88% and 1.50%. The mean SKR and QBER of each link are compared with the corresponding finite-key model pre- dictions as a function of total quantum channel loss in Fig. 4a.
